results.title: ML Reproducibility Tools and Best Practices | A minimal Hugo website
results.content: A recurrent challenge in machine learning research is to ensure that the presented and published results are reliable, robust, and reproducible [4,5,6,7]. Reproducibility, obtaining similar results as presented in a paper using the same code and data, is necessary to verify the reliability of research findings. Reproducibility is also an important step to promote open and accessible research, thereby allowing the scientific community to quickly integrate new findings and convert ideas to practice. In this blog post, we will share commonly used tools and explain 12 basic practices that you can use in your research to ensure reproducible science. Pytorch Lightning provides a great way to log all hyperparameters in `.csv` files in the experiment output folder, allowing for better reproducibility. Managing your model checkpoints is very important in terms of reproducibility, as it allows you to release trained models for the community to easily verify your work, as well as build upon it. Logging is also important for reproducibility, so researchers can verify the training progression of their replications in great detail. Probably the most important aspect of the exact reproducibility of your research is the seed of the experiment. Although exact reproducibility is not guaranteed, especially in GPU execution environments [2, 8], it’s still beneficial to report the seed due to its impact on your results. Before beginning your experiments, randomly draw \(n\) seeds and set them aside in your config file, and report all experimental results aggregated over those \(n\) seeds. When reporting your results, it is ideal to run your experiments in different seeds and/or different datasets. A higher bar of reproducibility is to report the results on *multiple datasets* to highlight the robustness of your model. While reporting your results, consult the ML Reproducibility Checklist which has detailed guidelines on the best practices for reporting figures and tables. You can also leverage headless virtual machines such as Docker or Singularity to provide the exact reproducible dev environment used for the experiments. This not only encourages reproducible research but also adds more visibility to your paper. Finally, it’s important from the reproducibility perspective to test your implementation in a *different environment* than the training setup.

results.title: PennyLane - Quantum: Machine Learning & Analytics
results.content: Published Time: 2020-05-16T14:20:30+00:00 PennyLane - Quantum: Machine Learning & Analytics PennyLane is a Python 3 software framework for optimization and machine learning of quantum and hybrid quantum-classical computations. The library provides a unified architecture for near-term quantum computing devices, supporting both qubit and continuous-variable paradigms. PennyLane’s core feature is the ability to compute gradients of variational quantum circuits in a way that is compatible with classical techniques such as backpropagation. PennyLane thus extends the automatic differentiation algorithms common in optimization and machine learning to include quantum and hybrid computations. A plugin system makes the framework compatible with any gate-based quantum simulator or hardware. On the classical front, PennyLane interfaces with accelerated machine learning libraries such as TensorFlow, PyTorch, and autograd. PennyLane can be used for the optimization of variational quantum eigensolvers, quantum approximate optimization, quantum machine learning models, and many other applications. Built-in automatic differentiation of quantum circuits. Support for hybrid quantum and classical models; connect quantum hardware with PyTorch, TensorFlow, and NumPy. Provides optimization and machine learning tools. The same quantum circuit model can be run on different backends. Install plugins to access even more devices, including Strawberry Fields, IBM Q, Google Cirq, Rigetti Forest, Microsoft QDK, and ProjectQ. * PennyLane-SF: Supports integration with Strawberry Fields, a full-stack Python library for simulating continuous variable (CV) quantum optical circuits. * PennyLane-qiskit: Supports integration with Qiskit, an open-source quantum computation framework by IBM. Provides device support for the Qiskit Aer quantum simulators, and IBM Q hardware devices. * PennyLane-cirq: Supports integration with Cirq, an open-source quantum computation framework by Google. * PennyLane-Forest: Supports integration with PyQuil, the Rigetti Forest SDK, and the Rigetti QCS, an open-source quantum computation framework by Rigetti. Provides device support for the the Quantum Virtual Machine (QVM) and Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) hardware devices. * PennyLane-Qsharp: Supports integration with the Microsoft Quantum Development Kit, a quantum computation framework that uses the Q# quantum programming language.

results.title: Version Control for ML Models: Best Practices and Tools
results.content: # Version Control for ML Models: Best Practices and Tools. Version control is fundamental in managing the complexity and evolution of machine learning (ML) models effectively. Unlike traditional software development, ML models evolve with data updates, feature engineering changes, and algorithmic improvements. This article explores the importance of version control for ML models, identifies best practices, and discusses essential tools to streamline versioning workflows. ### Why Version Control Matters for ML Models. ### Best Practices for Version Control in ML Models. Implementing effective version control for ML models involves adopting best practices tailored to the unique challenges of machine learning development:. * Git: Leverage Git for versioning model code, notebooks, and scripts. * MLflow: Use MLflow to track experiment metadata, including parameters, metrics, and artifacts (models, plots). MLflow supports integration with Git for versioning experiments and tracking model lineage. Docker images can encapsulate specific library versions, Python dependencies, and system configurations used for model training and deployment. * CI/CD Pipelines: Implement Continuous Integration (CI) and Continuous Deployment (CD) pipelines for automated model testing, validation, and deployment. * Model Registry: Use a centralized model registry, such as MLflow Model Registry or Kubeflow ModelDB, to catalog and manage model versions. * Versioning Data: Version datasets and data preprocessing pipelines alongside model code to maintain consistency between training and inference stages. * Git: Version control system for tracking changes in source code and project files. * MLflow Model Registry: Manages model versions, metadata, and deployment history. * MLflow Model Registry: Centralized repository for managing ML model versions and deployments. * Kubeflow ModelDB: Component of Kubeflow for tracking ML experiments, models, and metadata. Let’s outline a typical workflow using Git and MLflow for version control and experiment tracking:. Effective version control is essential for managing the lifecycle of ML models, ensuring reproducibility, collaboration, and reliability. By adopting best practices and leveraging tools like Git, MLflow, Docker, and CI/CD pipelines, organizations can streamline development workflows, mitigate risks, and accelerate model deployment. As ML continues to evolve, mastering version control methodologies will be crucial for maintaining agility and innovation in machine learning projects. results.content: Core Features of TFQ Cirq and Quantum Programming with Google Tools ProjectQ and Other Lightweight Frameworks Comparative Table: PennyLane vs TFQ vs Others Choosing the Right Framework for Your Use Case Quantum machine learning (QML) frameworks provide essential tools for building, training, and simulating quantum-enhanced models. Overview of QML Framework Categories * **Hybrid frameworks**: support classical-quantum integration (PennyLane, TFQ) * **Quantum-native frameworks**: focus purely on quantum simulation and programming (Qiskit, Cirq, Q#) * **Backend-agnostic tools**: allow switching between simulators and real quantum hardware 4. 9. Core Features of TFQ * Uses Cirq for circuit construction * Fully compatible with TensorFlow 2.x * Supports batching and hybrid quantum-classical models * Seamless integration with `tf.keras` API * Use of classical optimizers for training quantum circuits * Suitable for large-scale deep learning integration qubit = cirq.GridQubit(0, 0) circuit = cirq.Circuit(cirq.X(qubit)**0.5) quantum_layer = (circuit, cirq.Z(qubit))(model_input) * Part of IBM’s Qiskit ecosystem * Provides variational quantum classifiers, regressors, and quantum kernels * Compatible with Aer simulator and IBM Quantum hardware Cirq and Quantum Programming with Google Tools * Low-level circuit definition and execution * Basis for TFQ and Sycamore hardware programs * Good for research-level quantum circuit manipulation * Provides access to simulators and real QPUs (IonQ, Rigetti, OQC) * Python SDK for defining circuits and managing jobs * Supports hybrid workflows via PennyLane and PyTorch * Domain-specific language for quantum programming * Rich libraries for quantum chemistry and simulation * Less ML-focused but useful for custom quantum algorithm design ProjectQ and Other Lightweight Frameworks * Simpler interface for fast prototyping * Good for educational use and circuit visualization Comparative Table: PennyLane vs TFQ vs Others Choosing the Right Framework for Your Use Case * For hybrid ML research: **PennyLane** * For TensorFlow-based ML: **TFQ** * For IBM QPU access: **Qiskit ML** * For Google Sycamore: **Cirq/TFQ** * PennyLane: Active GitHub, forums, QHack community * TFQ: Backed by TensorFlow and Cirq teams * Qiskit: IBM-supported open-source initiative QML frameworks are vital for making quantum machine learning accessible and practical.

results.title: Xanadu | Training quantum neural networks with PennyLane, PyTorch, and TensorFlow
results.content: Xanadu | Training quantum neural networks with PennyLane, PyTorch, and TensorFlow. Accelerating Quantum Workflows with Xanadu's PennyLane and AMD | Learn more. Training quantum neural networks with PennyLane, PyTorch, and TensorFlow. Quantum machine learning in the NISQ era and beyond. Last year, we wrote about QML 1.0, our vision of the road ahead for quantum machine learning. Today, we can finally announce that **PennyLane****, our general-purpose library for quantum computing and machine learning, now integrates with****PyTorch****,****TensorFlow****,****Strawberry Fields****,****Forest** (Rigetti) **and****Qiskit** (IBM). PennyLane is the first software in the world to bring together the best of quantum computing with the best of machine learning. The links between quantum computing and machine learning go back several years. However, variational circuits have lately been extended more broadly into full-fledged general-purpose quantum machine learning algorithms. Unlike the more familiar quantum algorithms due to pioneers like Shor and Grover, the variational circuits paradigm has only been established in the past few years — largely because the NISQ era forced a rethink of quantum algorithms, but also due to the increasing cross-fertilization of quantum computing from machine learning. **QML 0.1: Porting quantum computing to machine learning**. The contemporary paradigm of quantum machine learning introduced above, i.e., quantum circuits as differentiable computations, is hugely promising. It was the first quantum simulator to offer all the machine learning goodies that TensorFlow provides, in particular the automatic differentiation and optimization features. > #### _“While the simulator route is useful for quantum machine learning in the short term, it is fundamentally not scalable.”_. While the simulator route is useful for quantum machine learning in the short term, it is fundamentally not scalable. **QML 1.0: Porting machine learning to quantum computing**. > #### _“Take all the best features from deep learning software and make them truly native to quantum devices.”_. Instead of simulating a quantum computer within conventional machine learning software, we would take all the best features from deep learning software and make them truly native to quantum devices. Example: Training a quantum circuit with PennyLane and PyTorch. Combining quantum computations and classical machine learning with PennyLane and PyTorch. This is just the tip of the iceberg for combining quantum computing with machine learning.
